h1: Deferred Adjudication & Defensive Driving Lawyer El Paso, TX
intro: Deferred disposition and the driving safety course are the two tools Texas law gives a Class C court to end a traffic ticket without a conviction. Both are in the judge's discretion and both have eligibility limits. Attorney Robert Navar requests the right one, after checking whether the ticket can simply be dismissed, for a flat fee from $59.
summaryHeading: Two ways an El Paso ticket can end without a conviction
summary: Deferred disposition (often called deferred adjudication) under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45A.302 (formerly art. 45.051): you enter a plea, the judge defers the case for up to 180 days on conditions and a court-set fee, and the case is dismissed if you complete them.

A driving safety course dismissal under art. 45A.352: an eligible driver pleads, takes a state-approved course, files the certificate and a driving record on time, and the case is dismissed. Not available for 25 mph or more over, CDL holders, or a course used in the past 12 months.
Neither is automatic. The statutes say the judge may grant them, and El Paso Municipal Court's page calls it "the judge's discretion" for anyone outside the by-right rules.
Texas no longer uses the former Driver Responsibility Program points system, repealed in 2019. What a deferral or course avoids today is the conviction itself.
Flat fees: $59 in El Paso Municipal Court, $69 in JP, Horizon City, Socorro and the smaller city courts. Hire online or call 915-503-1600.

sections.heading: Deferred Disposition in Plain Terms
paragraphs: Article 45A.302 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (formerly art. 45.051) lets a justice or municipal judge take your plea of guilty or no contest, decline to enter a judgment, and instead defer the case for a period the judge sets, not longer than 180 days. The judge can attach conditions: a special expense fee that may not exceed the fine for the offense, a driving safety course, proof of insurance, and the basic condition that you not be convicted of another traffic offense during the period. Complete everything and the judge dismisses the case. No conviction is reported to DPS.

The condition that trips people up is the clean period. A new citation anywhere in Texas that results in a conviction during the deferral can bring the case back before the judge, who may then enter the original conviction. The second thing people miss is the word "may": the statute gives the judge the power to defer, not the duty. A court can refuse, and a self-represented driver who has already pleaded is then left with a conviction. The statute also excludes certain offenses and, for a traffic offense in a motor vehicle, drivers who hold a commercial driver's license.

sections.heading: The Driving Safety Course in Plain Terms
paragraphs: Article 45A.352 (formerly art. 45.0511) is the other route, and it is more mechanical. A driver who qualifies asks the court, on or before the appearance date, to take a driving safety course; pleads guilty or no contest; pays court costs and an administrative fee set by the court; completes a state-approved course; and files the completion certificate and a certified Texas driving record within 90 days. The court then dismisses the case. El Paso Municipal Court's page lists what it wants back within its 90 days: a Type 3A certified driving record from DPS, the TDLR court copy of the completion certificate, and a copy of your insurance.

Eligibility is narrower than for deferral. In general you must be at least 17, hold a valid Texas driver's license (or be active military with a valid license), have proof of insurance, not hold a CDL, not have completed a course for a traffic offense in the preceding 12 months, and not be taking one for another pending ticket. Certain offenses are excluded outright: speeding 25 mph or more over the limit, a construction-zone violation with workers present, passing a stopped school bus, leaving the scene of an accident, fleeing an officer and reckless driving among them. Outside the by-right rules the course can still be requested, but the court's words are that it is the judge's discretion.

sections.heading: What Changed in 2019: The Former Points System
paragraphs: Older advice about defensive driving talks about keeping points off your license. That system is gone. The Driver Responsibility Program, which assigned points to convictions and charged annual surcharges, was repealed effective September 1, 2019, and outstanding surcharges were cancelled. Our explainer on the former Texas points system covers what was repealed.

What remains is the conviction. A traffic conviction may affect insurance premiums depending on the driver's history, carrier and other rating factors, and repeated moving-violation convictions can still affect a driver's record and may lead to a DPS license suspension in some circumstances. That is what a completed deferral or course keeps off the record.

sections.heading: Deferral vs. Course vs. Dismissal: Which to Ask For
paragraphs: The three are not interchangeable. An outright dismissal needs no plea, no fee and no waiting; it is the first thing to look for, and asking for a deferral or a course before anyone has checked the citation for a defect gives it up. Between the statutory options, the course is cheaper for an eligible first-time driver with a modest speed, while deferral reaches more cases: a driver who is 25 mph or more over, who used a course last year, or whose offense is on the excluded list can still ask for deferral, though the judge may decline. For a CDL holder, neither is legally available for a traffic offense, so the plan is a defect-based dismissal or a negotiated non-moving charge.

Robert Navar's office works in that order. We file an appearance and a not-guilty plea, review the citation for grounds to dismiss, and present those at pretrial in El Paso Municipal Court, the JP precincts or the city courts. Only when a dismissal is not available do we request deferral or the course. Our goal is to pursue the best available outcome based on the citation, driving record, court and circumstances. You do not have to appear; we send you the order with its deadlines.

sections.heading: What the Court Will Ask You to Do After It Grants a Deferral
paragraphs: A deferral order is a to-do list with dates on it. Pay the special expense fee by the date the court set. Keep proof of insurance current. Complete and file any course the judge required. Do not pick up another traffic conviction before the period ends. If the court set a compliance hearing, calendar it. When the period runs with the conditions met, the court dismisses the case. The court's file will still show the citation and the deferral; drivers who want that cleared may be eligible for an expunction after completion.

faqs.q: Is deferred adjudication the same as deferred disposition for a traffic ticket?
faqs.a: For Class C tickets the statutory term is deferred disposition under art. 45A.302, though many people and some courts say deferred adjudication. Either way it means a plea, a court-set period of up to 180 days with conditions, and a dismissal with no conviction if the conditions are met.

faqs.q: How long is the deferral period in El Paso?
faqs.a: The statute caps it at 180 days; the judge sets the length within that cap based on the charge and the driver's record.

faqs.q: Can I take defensive driving if I was going 25 over?
faqs.a: Not by right. Speeding 25 mph or more over the limit is excluded from the driving safety course dismissal. Those cases call for a deferral request or a negotiated reduction, each in the judge's discretion.

faqs.q: Does Texas still add points to my license for a ticket?
faqs.a: No. The former Driver Responsibility Program points system was repealed effective September 1, 2019. A conviction still goes on your driving record, which is what a completed deferral or course avoids.

faqs.q: What happens if I get another ticket during the deferral period?
faqs.a: A new conviction during the period can bring the case back before the judge, who may enter a conviction on the original charge. Call us right away; the new ticket can often be handled so it does not become a conviction before the deferral ends, though that depends on the second court.

faqs.q: Why not just request deferred disposition myself and save the fee?
faqs.a: Because the request is a plea that ends any chance of an outright dismissal, and the judge can decline it, leaving you with a conviction. For $59 to $69 we look for a dismissal first, then request a deferral or course with that leverage in hand.
